topics.title: Web page www.nervos.org - Discussion for new pull request

recent_posts.topic_title: Web page www.nervos.org - Discussion for new pull request
recent_posts.author: psawyerberlin
recent_posts.content_text:
Goal
nervos.org is often the first place newcomers, investors and developers look. This topic collects the community’s ideas for improving it.
For example, parts of the site still describe 2023: the “CKB Hardfork 2023” is listed as upcoming, Godwoken is recommended even though it was sunset, and the first halving is “expected around Nov 2023”.
The idea: collect the outdated content in one place, agree on the changes as a community, and turn them into a pull request, so the site reflects where CKB really is today.
How it would work
Proposed way forward:
Propose: the community suggests and discusses changes here in this topic.
Build: after a few weeks, a developer (myself and/or others) turns the agreed changes into code and opens a pull request on nervos-official-website.
Merge: a maintainer reviews and merges it, and the site is updated!
Maintainers, please correct me if the process is different.
In other words, nobody is to blame for the outdated site… or rather, we all are! Which also means any of us can help fix it.
What I’m asking for
Check the list below: anything missing, wrong, or no longer needed?
Help answer the open questions (Axon, UTXO Stack, Build Club / Grants).
Suggest what belongs in In progress and Upcoming for 2026–2027.
One rule: please avoid content that goes out of date quickly (prices, exact dates, version numbers). The site should stay easy to maintain.
Once there’s agreement, I’m happy to help prepare the pull request. Feel free to comment!

recent_posts.content_text:
Proposed changes
1. Journey page (nervos.org/journey)
Content last updated in July 2024.
Today
Proposed change
“CKB Hardfork 2023” under In progress and Upcoming
Move to Achievements: Meepo hard fork (CKB-VM v2), live on mainnet since 1 July 2025 (docs)
“CKB Fiber Testnet” under Upcoming
Move to Achievements: Fiber Network on mainnet (dev log); link fiber.world instead of the old cfn-node repo
“CKB Fiber (Lightning Network + CKB)” under In progress
Remove (covered by the item above)
Hidden Lorem ipsum placeholder descriptions
Remove
After these moves, In progress and Upcoming keep only items the core teams confirm. If nothing is confirmed, hide the section rather than show old items.
2. Foundation page
“Start with Godwoken” (“the easiest way to launch a dApp on Nervos!”): remove. Godwoken and Force Bridge were sunset in 2025 (announcement).
3. Mining page
“The first CKB halving is expected at Epoch 8760 (around Nov 2023)” → “The first halving took place in Nov 2023 (epoch 8760). Halvings happen every 8,760 epochs, about every four years.” (docs)
4. New links
Two useful community resources are missing from the site:
Resource
What it is
Proposed place
ckbccc.com
App built on CCC, the CKB developer library maintained by CKB DevRel
Developers → Developer Resources, next to CKB Docs
CKB Pulse by LusoCryptoLabs
Live view of who is building on CKB right now
Community → Get Involved (or Developers)
Open questions
These need an answer from someone who knows before they become changes:
Axon (home page, “Get Started”): “Launch your own Nervos sidechain with Axon” is one of three main calls to action. Is Axon still maintained? If not, what should replace it?
UTXO Stack (journey, “Upcoming”): has it launched, is it still planned, or should it be removed?
CKB Light Client (journey, “In progress”): “Light Client Soft Fork” is already under Achievements. Can “In progress” be removed?
Build Club / Grants Program (foundation page): are these still active? Should they point to the Community Fund DAO and the Spark Program instead?
In progress / Upcoming for 2026–2027: which items can the core teams confirm?
Your input: anything missing, wrong, or better placed elsewhere? Please keep suggestions to content that stays valid for at least a year.

recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] Fiber Desktop v1 ground-up rebuild and launch — fnn desktop app
recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
Fiber Studio v1.1.3 — fnn 0.9.1 and a channel neighborhood
Hi everyone,
Fiber Studio v1.1.3 is out. Two things changed.
The bundled node is now official fnn 0.9.1. Same node, newer pin. This release fixes on-chain settlement when a channel is force-closed, and funding failures come back with a clearer reason. Existing 0.9.0 node data still works. Upstream notes: fnn v0.9.1.
Network now shows your channel neighborhood instead of the gossip graph browser. Open Network and you get a map of your ready channels: your node, the peers you are connected to, and the public channels those peers have announced one step further. Scroll to zoom, drag to move, and click a public node to open one more step. A private channel stops at that peer, because nobody else can see it.
Screenshot 2026-11-05 at 21.56.462174×1270 90.2 KB
If you already have the app, go to Settings → Updates and install v1.1.3. Fresh installs are on the website.

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Light dApp Kit
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello, @Akane:
Thank you for taking the time to prepare and submit this proposal, and for your efforts on the browser light-client prototype.
The committee has completed its review. After careful discussion, we regret to inform you that the Light dApp Kit proposal will not be approved at this time.
We would like to be transparent about the reasons for this decision:
Duplication of existing ecosystem infrastructure: The CKB ecosystem already has a mature, production-ready product—NervDAO (https://nervdao.com/)—that fully supports deposits into and withdrawals from Nervos DAO. Building another DAO-focused dApp toolkit would essentially duplicate functionality that already exists.
Light-client tools already exist: CKB already provides an official browser-based WASM light client as a foundation, and the community has also built light-client projects on top of it.
“Validated value”: The Spark Program is intended to support exploratory projects that can bring incremental value to the CKB ecosystem. Since this proposal duplicates existing work, it falls outside Spark’s scope for validation.
We appreciate your team’s efforts on the prototype and proposal. Please keep building, and feel free to reach out to us anytime!
Best regards,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Project Committee

topics.title: Spark Program | CellFlow — Durable CCC Transaction Recovery PoC

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CellFlow — Durable CCC Transaction Recovery PoC
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello @Dangbaty2004,
Thank you for taking the time to submit the CellFlow proposal and provide detailed technical documentation. The committee has completed its review. We regret to inform you that the CellFlow proposal has been rejected at this time.
We would like to explain the reasons for this decision transparently:
The problem described may not reflect an actual need in the current ecosystem: CCC already supports transaction construction and signing, and CKB RPC supports querying transaction status. For the scenario described (inferring a transaction’s outcome after losing the broadcast response), the committee found insufficient evidence that CKB developers commonly encounter this kind of recovery issue when using CCC workflows.
The proposed solution adds architectural complexity and fragility: Requiring applications to adopt a PostgreSQL-based persistent reconciliation layer (including controlled fault injection and settlement logic) would impose a significant operational burden for edge-case failures. The committee believes this would make the system more fragile overall, rather than less. This concern has also been reflected in previous reviews (see the DevLaunch Kit precedent, which involved a mismatch in the fundamental concept): proposals that address non-core issues by adding complexity tend not to receive support.
We appreciate your team’s efforts on the proposal. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best regards,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

topics.title: Spark Program | TapFiber: Fiber Payment Intent and Verifiable Receipt Reference

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | TapFiber: Fiber Payment Intent and Verifiable Receipt Reference
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @vida,
Thank you for taking the time to submit the TapFiber proposal. The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to reject the TapFiber proposal at this time.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
Redundant with existing ecosystem work: The core concept of binding a Fiber payment intent to a merchant order and providing a verifiable payment receipt has already been implemented multiple times within the CKB ecosystem. Notably, Fiber Checkout—a Spark-funded and completed project—already provides a page-based payment solution for Fiber. The committee does not believe that rebuilding a similar payment-intent layer brings sufficient incremental value to justify further funding.
Overlapping scope with previously rejected proposals: The committee previously rejected Fiber Pay Studio (2026-07-21) for the same reason—the direction was deemed too similar to Fiber Checkout. TapFiber, while adding NFC as a physical delivery method, does not fundamentally differentiate itself from the existing payment flow infrastructure. NFC and QR are merely transport mechanisms; the underlying payment-request → settlement → receipt logic remains largely duplicative.
We appreciate the work your team has put into TapFiber — the commitment to reproducible tests and failure reporting is noted and commendable.
Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

recent_posts.author: LusoCryptoLabs
recent_posts.content_text:
An update since the post. Ward is now on npm as `ckb-ward` 0.1.0, with a browser entry for wallets and the verifier for platforms.
The Cellula wallet signs Ward proofs on testnet. A site asks, and the wallet shows which site is asking and for which account. It refuses a proof meant for another site or another network. We tested it today through the wallet’s own screen, with a starter account, a guarded account and a real phone passkey. Ward’s verifier accepted each proof, and refused a replay and a changed signature byte.
For Metaforo this means one verifier covers JoyID, multisig, Omnilock and smart account deposits. Happy to help wire it in.

topics.title: Spark Program | Spark Verify - Reproducible Acceptance Checks for CKB Projects

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Spark Verify - Reproducible Acceptance Checks for CKB Projects
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @Akane,
Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal based on our earlier feedback.
The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regrets to reject the Spark Verify proposal at this time.
We want to be transparent about the reasoning behind this decision:
The committee does not believe the project reduces the workload for developers and verifiers as claimed. The proposal describes a format for declaring observable results (committed/rejected transactions, cell states, balance changes, cycle usage) plus a runner to verify them on a local OffCKB devnet. However, the core problem — that verification instructions differ across projects and require manual judgment — is not meaningfully solved by introducing a new manifest format. A reviewer still needs to understand what the project claims to do, examine the verify.toml and accompanying scripts for correctness, and decide whether the assertions are adequate. In practice, the tool adds a layer of abstraction without removing the fundamental need for domain understanding and manual inspection. The committee’s question remains: who is the intended user, and does the tool actually save them time?
The manifest format risks becoming an additional maintenance burden rather than a labor-saving abstraction. Project authors would need to keep verify.toml in sync with their codebase as tool versions and setup details change. When a check fails, the author must debug whether the project, the toolchain, or the verify.toml itself is at fault. This is especially true given that OffCKB, CCC, and ckb-debugger are all actively iterating. The proposal pins versions, which is good, but even so, a failed run does not necessarily identify why it failed — which is precisely the “hard final acceptance step” the tool is meant to address.
We appreciate the work your team has put into Spark Verify. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

recent_posts.author: Akane
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @xingtianchunyan, thanks to you and the committee for reviewing the proposal.
I understand the decision. Whether the tool saves more effort than it adds is something real usage needs to answer.
I’ll continue CKB Verify independently. Its focus remains making declared acceptance checks easier to rerun and inspect, while reviewers still decide whether those checks are sufficient.
CKB Verify is open source under the MIT license, and anyone is free to use or adapt it. The repository includes runnable examples and setup instructions for Linux x64:
https://github.com/Akane-CN/spark-verify
If you try it, I’d appreciate feedback on what helped and what made the workflow harder. Issues and PRs are welcome.

topics.title: Noir-CKB: the private tally is live on CKB testnet, try it yourself

recent_posts.topic_title: Noir-CKB: the private tally is live on CKB testnet, try it yourself
recent_posts.author: xiaomao
recent_posts.content_text:
GM,
This is a new chapter of noir-ckb, so a quick catch-up first. In my direction check (Direction check: should noir-ckb generate CKB Type Scripts from Noir circuits?) I asked whether noir-ckb should generate CKB Type Scripts from Noir circuits. In the follow-up (Noir-CKB update: what I decided after the direction check, what you can try today, and where this is going) I shared what I decided, and since then I’ve posted updates there as the private tally took shape and its setup ceremony ran to the end.
The private tally is now deployed on testnet, and anyone can create their own. A three-minute recording of the full run:
What the private tally is
A CKB Cell that holds a hidden number. Only the holder of a secret key can add to it, and every addition is authorized by a zero-knowledge proof made on their own computer.
- The Cell stores only a commitment: a fingerprint of the number, made with fresh randomness each time, so it reveals nothing about the value.
- You can add any amount, including 0. A “cover update” looks exactly like a real one, so even “did anything change?” stays private.
- There is no signature lock on the tally. The proof is the only authority.
How it works: the proof is bound to one exact transition
A valid proof on its own is not enough. If the Type Script accepted any valid proof, someone could copy one from the mempool and use it on a different Cell. So the Type Script doesn’t trust the proof’s public values. It rebuilds them from the actual transaction:
- the network,
- the exact Cell being consumed,
- the old and the new commitment,
- the lock and capacity of the new Cell,
and it hashes all of that into the proof’s public input. A proof is therefore valid for exactly one transition of exactly one Cell. Used anywhere else, it fails.
Before anything went on testnet, this was tested in CKB-VM with 49 attack cases (all rejected as expected): replaying a proof on another Cell or another network, swapping commitments, wrong or altered verification keys, malformed witnesses and more. 4 mutation tests then removed one safety check at a time to confirm the tests notice when it is missing.
Why there was a ceremony
Groth16 needs a proving key made with secret randomness, and whoever kept that randomness could forge proofs. Because the proof is the only authority here, a key made by me alone would have meant trusting me completely.
So I ran a public phase 2 setup ceremony. Four people contributed, every key was verified, and the result was sealed with the hash of CKB mainnet block 20,870,000. Nobody can forge proofs as long as at least one contributor threw their randomness away. Thank you, truthixify, alienate, and Cecilia. The transcript is public and can be re-checked with one command: [ceremony folder](noir-ckb-verifier/ceremony/private-tally-v2 at main · wamimi/noir-ckb-verifier · GitHub).
The deployed verification key is that ceremony’s key, and the join tool checks this on your own machine before you use it.
What it looks like on testnet
I created a tally, added 7, then added 0.
value_73024×198 16.7 KB
update3018×112 32.7 KB
value_03022×208 18.5 KB
One of these updates added 7, the other added nothing. On chain they have the same size and shape: one 33-byte commitment replaced by another, plus a proof. The ~117 million cycles are the Groth16 verification running in CKB-VM. The value 7 exists only in my private folder.
Step
Transaction
Deploy (Type Script, ceremony verification key, guard lock)
0x39ef90b8…47b1f9
Create at 0
0x58d64623…6eca67
Add a hidden amount (7)
0xa93b9ed5…1c4a73
Cover update (0)
0xbc062ecc…66046c
A second account then joined the same deployment with its own key and added a hidden amount, the same way you would.
What it does not hide
Anyone can see that a tally exists, when and how often it was updated, and which account paid the fee, and one tally’s updates are linkable to each other. What stays private is the value and every amount added.
Try it
If you’re a developer, you can create your own hidden tally on this deployment and watch it happen on testnet. It costs about 262 testnet CKB (free from the faucet), there is nothing to deploy, and every proof is made on your machine.
After installing git, Python, Node.js and rustup, it is two commands from inside the cloned repository:
```bash
python3 -B scripts/try-private-tally.py install
python3 -B scripts/try-private-tally.py run
```
`install` lists everything it will set up and asks once. `run` rebuilds the proving setup from the ceremony key, checks the deployment, makes a testnet-only account, waits for your faucet payment, then creates your tally and lets you add hidden amounts. It shows every transaction and asks before signing and sending it; your password only ever goes to `ckb-cli`.
Guide: noir-ckb-verifier/docs/try-the-private-tally.md at main · wamimi/noir-ckb-verifier · GitHub
Supported: macOS on Apple silicon and Linux (x86_64, ARM64). The first run takes about 20–30 minutes, most of it downloading and compiling.
What I’d love to hear
1. Did it work on your machine? Where did you get stuck?
2. What would you build with this, and what would you want a proof like this bound to?
The next step for noir-ckb is turning these examples into a toolkit you can install and use for your own Noir circuits, with the CKB binding generated for you. Your answers will shape it.

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | NNCBN - Nervos Network Community Boot Nodes
recent_posts.author: NNCBN
recent_posts.content_text:
IN PROGRESS until November 10
2026 November, Seventh Weekly Report
Qubes has been updated to the latest version: Initial observations on data usage on-site. A dom0 update required 1,000 MB—it was actually a little over 500 MB—but when combined with the fedora-44-xfce update, about 1,200 MB were needed. Another small dom0 update today used about 80 MB of data.
Time settings
Since we’re setting up an Internet node, it’s important that the time is accurate! Once the device is in place, we’ll make sure the system settings are up to date.
In dom0 terminal
timedatectl status
Compare the time listed under “Universal Time” with the actual UTC time. If the UTC time shown there is wrong:
qubes-prefs clockvm
The ClockVM (usually sys-net) should be running and have network access. Than run:
sudo qvm-sync-clock
Afterwards set the system time zone:
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Atlantic/
Find valid names with timedatectl list-timezones
The terminal command timedatectl status must display the correct times.

recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello, @NOrththebear,
Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal based on our earlier feedback. The committee has completed its review and, after careful discussion, regretfully decided to reject the Bees Network proposal at this time.
We would like to be transparent about the reasons for this decision:
Outside the scope of Spark grants: In the committee’s assessment, the success of Bees Network depends heavily on bootstrapping network effects, providing ongoing incentives for node operations, and acquiring demand from AI agents. This type of project is long-term, operations-driven infrastructure and involves significant uncertainty.
We appreciate your team’s efforts on Bees Network—deploying an MVP on the Pudge testnet and clearly explaining how CKB’s Cell Model can be applied to reward accounting are both commendable. Keep building, and feel free to reach out anytime!
Best，
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Project Committee

recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_html:
Thanks for reaching out,

my suggestion would be, that before real funds enter, prioritise three additional acceptance runs:

  1. a cross-LSP payment interrupted after the recipient’s credit is committed but before upstream completion, followed by a process crash and retry of the same invoice;

  2. a partition carried through forced closure, testing both preimage claims and timeout refunds;

  3. a wallet exit with the LSP, gateway and operator watchtower all unavailable, using only recovery material already held by the user and an independent CKB endpoint.
